Build first; every item listed above depends on it. All four primitives are model-agnostic: they take plain data, so they import nothing from src/lib.

OutcomeGroups:
- Props: groups {id, title, runCount, lines {time?: string; text: string}[], endState?: string, badge?: string}[]; firstDivergentStep?: number; capped?: boolean; runCount: number; onSelect?(groupId) so the caller can load that run into its own scrubber.

- Cards are buttons; an aria-live line summarises the count. At 390 px the cards stack.

ReorderList:
- Props: items {id, label, description?}[], order: string[], onChange(order), label, lockedIds?, marks? Record<id, 'correct' | 'wrong'> (shown only after the caller reveals).
- Each row has Move up and Move down buttons (at least 40 px tall, disabled at the ends). An aria-live region announces 'X moved to position n of m'. No drag-only interaction.

MutationMatrix:
- Props: rows {id, label}[], columns {id, label}[], cells Record<'row:col', {state: 'caught' | 'survived' | 'not-run'; summary?: string}>, predictions?, onPredict?(row, col, value), revealed: boolean, onCellSelect?(row, col).

- Real table semantics with row and column headers; the table scrolls inside its own panel at 390 px.

BitStrip:
- Props: bits ('0' | '1' | 'x' | 'z')[] MSB first, label, extendedFrom?, signBit?, droppedFrom?, segments? {hi, lo, label, tone}[] (struct members, byte lanes), highlight? and changed? index sets, undefinedBits? (a distinct 'undefined' texture, never the X hatch), bitNumbers?: boolean, ascending?: boolean (for [0:15] declarations).

Export all four (plus their prop types) from src/components/visual-system/index.ts. Tests: one file covering keyboard reordering and announcements, the capped notice, prediction gating in MutationMatrix and the x/z encodings in BitStrip.

components.modelRules:
IEEE 1800-2023.

Event controls (sv-event-control-model.ts):
- edgeOf(old, new) over 0/1/x/z per Table 9-2. Posedge: 0->1, 0->x, 0->z, x->1, z->1. Negedge: 1->0, 1->x, 1->z, x->0, z->0.
- posedge and negedge look at the least significant bit only, and a change of an operand that leaves the expression's value unchanged is not an event (9.4.2).
- 'or' and ',' are equivalent event OR operators (9.4.2.1).
- An iff guard is evaluated when the event expression changes and must be true per 12.4, so x/z is false; iff binds tighter than or (9.4.2.3).
- sv-process-model uses only the 0/1/X subset.

Procedures:
- No implied order between initial and always procedures (9.2); ready processes run in any order (4.7).
- always_comb is triggered once at time zero, after all initial and always procedures have started, and then on changes of what it reads. The inferred sensitivity excludes variables declared or written in the block and names used only in timing controls (9.2.2.2, 9.2.2.2.1). always @* waits for a change (9.2.2.2.2).
- NBA updates land after every time-0 procedure has run to its first timing control (4.5, 4.9.4, 10.4.2).

Initializers:
- A static variable's declaration initializer is set before any initial or always procedure starts (6.8, 10.5). 'It produces no event' is derived from that (no procedure exists yet to see it); label it 'derived from 6.8'.
- The 1364-2005 behaviour comes only from the 6.8 NOTE and is labelled that way.

Severity and end of run:
- $info, $warning and $error print a tool-specific message and return; $fatal makes an implicit call to $finish (20.10).
- $stop suspends simulation (20.2), so finals do not run then.
- $finish exits (20.2); final procedures run when simulation ends 'due to an explicit or implicit call to $finish', in zero time, and no remaining scheduled events run (9.2.3).
- Model assumption, shown in the UI: 9.6.1 says simulation 'automatically terminates when there is no further activity of any kind' but does not say whether finals run then. The existing model runs them; relabel that narration 'model assumption', since 9.2.3 does not state it.

Other:
- The zero-delay infinite loop is 9.2.2.1 (the existing zero-delay-loop outcome).
- while treats an x/z condition as false (12.7.4, 12.4).
- 'horizon' and the cap are model concepts, labelled as such.
- Out of scope: intra-assignment timing (TimingControlExplorer) and continuous assignments.

components.modelRules:
IEEE 1800-2023.

Conditional and if:
- With an x/z condition, both expressions are evaluated and compared for logical equivalence (11.4.5). If that comparison is 1, either one is returned; otherwise they are combined bit by bit with Table 11-20 (11.4.11).
- Table 11-20 keeps a bit only where both branches hold the same known value (0 with 0, 1 with 1). Every other pair is x, including x with x and z with z.
- The existing evaluator already implements exactly this (the cond case near L1105); the UI wording must say 'agree on 0 or 1'.
- 12.4: if treats an x/z condition as false and takes else.

Bit-vector functions (20.9):
- $countbits(e, control bits) counts the bits that match a control value; x bits never count as 1.
- $countones(e) = $countbits(e,'1) and returns int.
- $onehot is $countbits(e,'1)==1; $onehot0 is <=1; $isunknown is $countbits(e,'x,'z)!=0. All three return bit.

Concatenation:
- 11.4.12: members are self-determined, joined MSB first, and the result is unsigned; an unsized constant inside braces is illegal.
- 11.4.12.1: the replication count is a constant. A concatenation may be an assignment target; a replication may not.

Casts and signedness:
- 6.24.1: a size cast pads or truncates and keeps signedness; signed'() keeps the bits and changes their meaning.
- 11.8.1: part-selects and concatenations are unsigned; simple decimals are signed; based literals are unsigned unless written with s.
- 11.3.3: -'d12 / 3 is unsigned arithmetic.
- 11.8.2: evaluation steps (context width, then type propagation).
- 11.4.10: >>> fills with the sign bit only when the expression is signed.
- 11.6.2: the bit-length example.

Literals (5.7.1):
- Fill literals set every bit and are 1 bit wide when self-determined.
- A leftmost x or z digit pads with x or z to the size of the containing expression. The clause's own example: 'hx assigned to an 85-bit target gives 85 x bits.

New component on a new pure model. Build after OutcomeGroups; it imports BitStrip, ReorderList and MutationMatrix from visual-system. Integrator: MDX tag PackedLayoutExplorer.

Props: mode 'struct' (default) | 'union' | 'tagged' | 'mutation' | 'debug'; preset?: string.

struct mode:
- A BitStrip, MSB on the left, with one segment per member labelled [hi:lo], plus the $bits total.
- Members are reordered with ReorderList and their widths edited (1-16 bits).
- Presets:
  - cmd_t: op[31:28], addr[27:16], data[15:0];
  - ctrl_reg_t;
  - frame_t (the interview question);
  - pkt_hdr_t (the kata), highlighting that kind and seq share one hex digit;
  - 'reversed addr/data';
  - 'narrow assign';
  - 'enum field', with opcode_e op.
- Predict sequence on cmd_t:

components.modelRules:
IEEE 1800-2023.

Rounding and units:
- 3.14: the precision may not be coarser than the unit.
- 3.14.1: delays are rounded to the element's own precision, and a finer precision elsewhere does not help. Its example: 2.75 ns at 1ns/100ps becomes 2.8 ns. No tie rule is stated; handle ties as described in the spec.
- 5.8: a time literal is scaled to the current time unit, then rounded.
- 6.12.1: converting a real to an integer rounds to nearest with an exact .5 away from zero. This applies to passing 1.5 to a time argument.
- 9.4.1: an x/z delay is treated as zero; a negative delay is interpreted as a two's-complement unsigned integer of the same size as a time variable.

Which unit applies:
- 3.14.2.1: a `timescale applies to later design elements of the same compilation unit until another `timescale or a `resetall (22.3).
- 3.12.1: how files map to compilation units is tool-specific.
- 3.14.2.2: timeunit and timeprecision keywords.
- 3.14.2.3: precedence (a) nested elements inherit from the enclosing module or interface; (b) the last earlier `timescale in the compilation unit; (c) a compilation-unit timeunit; (d) the implementation default. It is an error if some design elements specify a unit and precision and others do not.
- 3.14.3: the global precision is the minimum over all timeprecision statements, all timeunit precision arguments and the smallest `timescale precision; 1step equals it.
- 20.4.2: $printtimescale.

Reading time:
- 20.3.1: $time is an integer in the caller's unit, rounded. Its example: #1.55 at 10ns/1ns lands at 16 ns and 32 ns, and $time reports 2 and 3.
- 20.3.2: $stime returns the low 32 bits.
- 20.3.3: $realtime keeps the fraction.
- 20.4.3 with Tables 20-2 and 20-3: $timeformat governs %t until the next call; the defaults are units = the smallest `timescale precision, precision 0, a null suffix and minimum width 20.

Assumption stated in the UI: 20.4.3 and 21.2.1.2 do not settle how a %0t field width interacts with minimum_field_width.

Lifetime and storage:
- 13.3.2: all items of a static task are static, with one copy per module instance shared by concurrent activations; they keep their values between calls and start at their defaults. IEEE 1800-2023.

Case family:
- 12.5: case compares with a 4-state exact match, items in source order, and the first match executes. With no match and no default, nothing executes and nothing is reported.
- 12.5.1: casez treats z/? as don't-care in both the expression and the items; casex treats x and z as don't-care in both.

Qualifiers:
- 12.5.3 (unique, unique0): two or more matching case items is a violation; the first matching item still executes. Comparisons continue after the first match. One case item that lists several matching expressions is not an overlap.
- 12.5.3 (no match): unique and priority report it; unique0 does not. A default item is itself a case item, so with a default present there is no no-match report.
- 12.4.2: the same rules apply to unique-if, unique0-if and priority-if chains, conditions may be evaluated in any order for unique and unique0, and a final else removes the no-match report.

case inside:
- 12.5.4: each item is compared with the inside operator, the case expression as the left operand. A result of 1'b1 is a match; 1'b0 and 1'bx are no match.
- 11.4.13: inside uses ==? for singular values and <= / >= for ranges.
- 11.4.6: wildcard matching is asymmetric: x/z/? in the right operand are wildcards; x/z in the left operand are not.
- 11.4.4: a relational comparison with an x operand gives x.

Reporting: 12.4.2.1 and 12.5.3.1: the check runs when the statement executes, and the report is deferred to the Observed region of the current time step.

How a run ends and how time advances.
- Severity tasks report but do not end the run; $fatal ends it; $stop suspends it; final runs in zero time.

- 9.3.2: join_any resumes the parent when any branch ends.
- 9.6.3: disable fork kills every descendant.
- 4.5: time advances only by moving to the first nonempty time slot.
- 9.6.1: simulation terminates when there is no further activity of any kind. Whether finals run then is unstated, so it is labelled a model assumption.
- 9.2.2.1: zero-delay infinite loop.
- 12.7.4: while.

components.modelRules:
IEEE 1800-2023.

Files:
- 21.3.1: $fopen returns 0 when the file cannot be opened.
- 21.3.4.3: $fscanf skips white space (newlines included), returns the number of items successfully matched and assigned, and returns 0 on an early mismatch, leaving the offending character unread. EOF (-1) is returned only if the input ends before the first successful conversion or match. Trailing white space, including the final newline, is left unread.
- 21.3.4.2: $fgets reads one line.
- 21.3.8: $feof returns nonzero only after a read has already reached the end.
- 20.10: $error prints and returns; $fatal implies $finish. 20.2: $finish.
- 11.4.5: !== compares including x and z.

Plusargs (21.6):
- matching is by prefix;
- plusargs are searched in command-line order, and the first match wins;
- a miss returns 0, leaves the variable unchanged and warns nobody;
- on a match the remainder is converted with the format, and an empty remainder stores zero or an empty string;
- characters the format cannot convert write 'bx, so a 4-state variable reads X while an int silently becomes 0.

The tests cite these clauses and reproduce the lesson's summary lines.

triage:
- Five rounds in shuffled order. Each shows a model-generated log and end state with the code hidden:
  - the end time;
  - whether time stopped advancing (a zero-delay loop) or the run ended quietly;
  - the call each blocked process is stuck in.
- The learner names the smell.
- The reveal shows the code, the blocked lanes, the governing clause and the fix; HintLadder with three hints; then 'apply fix and rerun' shows the log complete.
- Scenario sources:
  - missed trigger: the existing eventRaceScenario('at-trigger');
  - spinning on triggered: eventRaceScenario('triggered-loop');
  - leaked key: keyLeakScenario('bug');
  - circular wait: the new circularWaitScenario;
  - starved consumer: the new starvedConsumerScenario (consumer repeat(4) vs 3 puts).

deadlock:
- Toggle proc_b's acquisition order (s2 then s1, or s1 then s2) and its start delay (0 or 10 ns). The delay shows that opposite orders deadlock only when the critical sections overlap.
- PREDICT: hangs forever / both finish / depends on process order.
- Step a wait-for graph (WaitForGraph.tsx): process -> the semaphore it waits on; semaphore -> the process holding its key. The cycle closes in rose at 5 ns, and 'every legal order' (OutcomeGroups) confirms the hang.
- Holder edges carry the label 'model bookkeeping: a semaphore does not track owners'.
- The same-order variant shows proc_b queued FIFO behind proc_a, and both finish.
- Cycle detection reuses listCycles from src/lib/axi-deadlock-model.ts (map each edge to {from, to, legality: 'legal', explanation}) instead of a second implementation (critic point).

kata:
- Shown only after the worked-solution reveal. The starter runs in the model across every legal order and shows two outcomes at 30 ns (report line printed / not printed), with chk blocked in its fourth get().
- Two independent fix toggles: 'N shared' and '@(mon_done) waited from 0 ns'. Each smell disappears separately.
components.modelRules:
IEEE 1800-2023:
- 15.5.1 and 15.5.2: -> unblocks only processes already waiting.
- 15.5.3: triggered stays true until simulation time advances, so a zero-delay loop on it never ends.
- 15.3.2: put returns keys. 15.3.3: get blocks and waiters queue FIFO.
- 15.4.5: mailbox get blocks while the mailbox is empty.
- 4.7: processes ready together run in any order.
- 9.6.1: a run with only blocked processes ends quietly (no further activity).

Scenario builders live in sv-ipc-smell-scenarios.ts and use only sv-process-model statements; never edit sv-process-model.ts. Exploration uses exploreProcessOrders with signature 'timestamps' and onCap 'mark'.

Semaphores do not record owners (15.3), so holder edges are bookkeeping. The existing SemaphoreSnapshot.held is already documented that way.

New 2D component on a new pure select model. This resolves the critic's 3D point: one-dimensional selects and the query functions are 2D, and only the mem[16] block keeps a 3D scene (a separate SystemVerilog3DVisualizer item that imports this model). Build after OutcomeGroups, for BitStrip. Integrator: MDX tag ArraySelectExplorer.

Props: mode 'select' (default) | 'part-select' | 'query'; preset?: string.

select. Arrays, with their values given so every prediction is answerable:
- w = logic [3:0][7:0] holding 32'hAABB_CCDD;
- b = logic [7:0] b[4] = '{8'h11, 8'h22, 8'h33, 8'h44};
- mem = logic [3:0][7:0] mem[16] with mem[i][j] = 8'((i << 4) | j), so mem[5] = 32'h5352_5150, mem[5][2] = 8'h52 and mem[5][2][3] = 1'b0;
- grid = int grid[4][8] with grid[r][c] = 10*r + c.
Select chips: w, w[2], w[3:2], w[2][3], w[23:16], b[1], b[1:2], b[5], b[i] with i = x, mem[5], mem[5][2], mem[5][2][3], grid[1], grid[1][7].
- PREDICT the value and its kind (packed vector / unpacked slice / single bit / x) first.
- Then the selected cells light up: a BitStrip with byte-lane segments for packed data, separate boxes for unpacked elements, and a rows-by-lanes grid for mem. The value and its type appear.
- A logic/bit toggle shows invalid reads as 'x vs '0.
- w[23:16] shows the 11.5.1 result (x when read), with the lesson's 'many tools warn or reject at compile time (tool-dependent)' note.

part-select:
- A 32-bit v with an i slider: PREDICT which byte v[8*i +: 8] covers; also v[15 -: 8].
- Then flip the declaration to logic [0:15] up_vect and predict again: up_vect[0 +: 8] is up_vect[0:7]. That is the most significant byte only because base 0 is the MSB of an ascending range; the select still runs from the base toward the higher index numbers (bitNumbers + ascending BitStrip).
- A partially out-of-range select reads x for the missing bits.

query:
- Arrays: int f[7:0]; a queue of 3; an empty queue; an assoc with keys 5 and 9; an empty assoc; the tracker `bit [31:0] exp_by_id [int][$]` with keys 5 and 9 holding queues of 2 and 1.
- Pick a dimension number (buttons). PREDICT $left, $right, $low, $high, $increment, $size, $dimensions and $unpacked_dimensions, then reveal.
- A 2D layout draws the dimensions as nested columns: a sparse key column with gaps, ragged queue rows, and 32-bit chips. $size(exp_by_id, 2) shows the illegal-dimension error; $size(exp_by_id[5], 1) is legal.
components.modelRules:
IEEE 1800-2023.

Selects:
- 7.4.4 and 7.4.5: in an element select the unpacked indices come first, then the packed ones; the rightmost index varies fastest. A slice of a packed array is packed; a slice of an unpacked array is unpacked. For logic [3:0][7:0], bit = p1*8 + p2, so w[2][3] is bit 19.
- Invalid reads:
  - Packed (fixed from the draft): 11.5.1 governs bit-selects, part-selects and packed-array selects. An invalid bit-select reads x for 4-state and 0 for 2-state values. A part-select completely out of range, or with x/z, reads x; a partially out-of-range one reads x for the out-of-range bits. Invalid writes have no effect.
  - Unpacked: 7.4.5 and Table 7-1 govern invalid indexes into unpacked arrays: 'x for a 4-state element, '0 for a 2-state element.
- 11.5.1, indexed part-selects (fixed from the draft): `v[base +: w]` selects w bits starting at the base and ascending the bit range; `-:` descends.
  - On an ascending range ([0:15]) the base is the msb_base_expr, so higher index numbers are less significant bits.
  - The standard's example: b_vect[0 +: 8] == b_vect[0:7], and b_vect[15 -: 8] == b_vect[8:15].

Query functions:
- 20.7: $left/$right/$low/$high/$increment/$size/$dimensions/$unpacked_dimensions, with dimensions numbered from the slowest-varying, which is 1.
- 20.7.1: queries over multiple variable dimensions; $size(exp_by_id, 2) is illegal.
- 7.11: array querying functions for dynamic arrays, queues and associative arrays. For an int-keyed associative array, $right is the largest possible index, not the largest key; the lesson states this, and a test pins it against the 7.11/20.7 text.

Precedence:
- 11.3.2 with Table 11-2: precedence and associativity. Unary operators bind tightest, so -2 ** 2 is (-2) ** 2. All binary operators group left to right except ?: (right to left). == binds tighter than the binary & ^ |, and + binds tighter than <<.

Width:
- 11.6 and Table 11-21: expression bit lengths.
- 11.6.2: the bit-length example.
- 11.8.2: evaluation steps. The context width is the largest of the context-determined operands and the assignment target; self-determined operands are sized alone; the operands of a relational or equality operator size each other and the result is 1 bit.

IEEE 1800-2023:
- 6.5: a variable may be written by one continuous assignment or by procedural code, not both, and the rule applies per longest-static-prefix element. A declaration initializer counts as a procedural write. An instance output port connected to a variable is an implied continuous assignment.

Directed:
- Toggle the lesson's three tests, or build a fourth as a step list (for example: reset, load 7, then ld+en with d = 3).

components.concept: Deferred reporting. A unique/priority violation check, or a deferred assertion, runs when its statement executes, but the report waits in that process's queue. A flush point discards it: the procedure resuming after an event control, or an always_comb re-triggered by an input. components.modelRules:
IEEE 1800-2023.

Violation reports:
- 12.4.2.1 and 12.5.3.1: the check is evaluated when the statement executes, and reporting is deferred to the Observed region. The pending report sits on a queue for the executing process.
- Flush points: the procedure resumes after an event control or wait; or an always_comb/always_latch resumes on a transition of a dependent signal. Flushing discards pending reports.
- In Observed each pending report matures and can no longer be flushed; the tool-specific report mechanism then reports it.

Deferred assertions:
- 16.4.1: pending reports per process. Observed-deferred reports mature in Observed and their action runs in Reactive; final-deferred reports mature in Postponed. A Reactive-to-Active loop can still glitch an observed deferred assertion.
- 16.4.2: deferred assertion flush points.

Assertion control (20.11, Tables 20-5 and 20-6):
- Off (4): queued violation reports are not flushed and may still mature, but no new ones are queued. Kill (5): aborts; verify Kill's exact effect on queued violation reports in 20.11 before writing the narration.
- assertion_type: 32 Unique, 64 Unique0, 128 Priority (so 224 covers all three).

components.spec:
New component on two small pure models. Integrator: MDX tag PrintingLab.

format mode:
- Choose a width (4, 9 or 12 bits); toggle each bit through 0/1/x/z; choose %d, %0d, %h, %0h, %o or %b.
- PREDICT the exact text in a row of character cells, with spaces shown as a dot.
- The reveal shows:
  - 4-bit or 3-bit group brackets over the bit strip;
  - each group mapped to its character, with the rule that fired (all x gives x, some x gives X, z gives Z unless an x is present);
  - the width calculation (for 12 bits, 4095 needs 4 decimal columns and FFF needs 3 hex columns).
- Presets: r1 = 10 on 12 bits (the lesson's padding line); 4'b10x1; all z; x and z in one digit.

monitor mode:
- A 0-60 ns slot axis, lanes for a and b, and the active watch list drawn as a band that changes at each new $monitor call.
- PREDICT for each slot: prints or silent, and the exact line.
- Controls: move or delete the second $monitor call; add b to the first list; insert $monitoroff or $monitoron at a time; switch to $fmonitor, which keeps two lists active.
- The reveal shows Postponed print markers, one collapsed line for the double change at 20 ns, and silence at 30 ns (b is not watched, and $time does not count).
- Preset 'replaced-list' is debug case 1: the log stops showing a signal after a second $monitor call. Pick the suspect line and a fix; the model reruns.
components.modelRules:
IEEE 1800-2023.

Format:
- 21.2.1.2: the field width for an expression is sized to the largest possible value, with leading spaces for decimal and leading zeros for hex/octal/binary; %0 gives the minimum width.
- 21.2.1.3: a hex/octal digit whose bits are all x prints x and all z prints z; a digit with some x (and no z?) prints X, and a mixed digit with z prints Z; decimal values containing x/z follow the same table. Encode the clause's own table, with tests per row.

$monitor:
- 21.2.3: one $monitor list is active at a time and a new call replaces it. It prints at the end of a time slot in which any listed argument changed, except changes of $time, $stime and $realtime. $monitoron and $monitoroff control it, and $monitoron prints at once.
- 21.3.2: any number of $fmonitor lists may be active.
- 4.4.2.9: Postponed.

Accuracy caveat (kept from the audit): the normative text of 21.2.3 does not say that the $monitor call itself prints a first line; the 20.3.1 example output shows one ('0 set=x'). The model cites that example and labels the behaviour 'as shown in the 20.3.1 example', because the lesson's rows at 0 ns and 40 ns depend on it.

The file pane comes from presets: the lesson's rom.hex; '@4 aa bb'; '@10' (address 16, because @ is hex); a short file; '8'h12' (an error); an @ outside the given range. Start and finish arguments are settable (none / start only / start > finish).

components.modelRules:
IEEE 1800-2023, 21.4:
- With no addresses, loading starts at the lowest address and moves upward; with only a start address it moves upward from there; with start greater than finish it moves downward. The direction holds after an @ line.
- @ addresses are hexadecimal.
- Unreached locations are not modified.
- Numbers may not carry a size or a base.
- When the system task specifies an address range, an @ address outside it is an error and loading ends.
- When start and finish are given and the file has no @ lines, a word-count mismatch is a warning.
Tests cite each rule; verify every rule against the 21.4 text before encoding it.
